primer.rus_p_world.title: Land of the Rurikids
primer.rus_p_world.text: You were born in Rus - a land of forests, rivers and wooden towns. It is ruled by princes of the house of Rurik: according to the chronicle, in 862 the Slavs invited the Varangian Rurik "to rule and reign over them", and his descendants have held the princely thrones for over seven centuries. A prince judges, collects tribute and leads his druzhina, his warband, to war. The roads here are rivers: in summer boats sail them, and in winter sledges run over the ice.
primer.rus_p_world_vladimir.title: The baptism of Rus
primer.rus_p_world_vladimir.text: Vladimir Sviatoslavich reigns in Kiev. At first he set up idols of Perun and other gods on a hill, but around 988 he was baptised himself, married the Byzantine princess Anna and had the people of Kiev baptised in the Dnieper. His son Yaroslav the Wise (secure in Kiev from 1019) builds the Cathedral of Saint Sophia, writes down the first laws - the Russkaya Pravda - and marries his daughters to the kings of France, Norway and Hungary. Rus is one of the largest realms in Europe.
primer.rus_p_world_appanage.title: Princes divide Rus
primer.rus_p_world_appanage.text: After Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, his sons and grandsons divided Rus, and the princes keep fighting over the best thrones. In 1097 at a congress in Lyubech they agreed that "each shall hold his own patrimony" - but the peace did not last. Vladimir Monomakh (1113–1125) united Rus once more against the Polovtsians, and then it broke into a dozen principalities. The strongest is the land of Vladimir-Suzdal: in 1169 the army of Andrei Bogolyubsky stormed and plundered Kiev.
primer.rus_p_world_horde.title: The Horde yoke
primer.rus_p_world_horde.text: The Mongols have come - in Rus they are called Tatars. In 1237–1240 Khan Batu burned Ryazan, Vladimir and Kiev, and Rus became a tributary of the Golden Horde. Now a prince may take his throne only with the khan's yarlyk, a patent, and to get it he must travel to Sarai on the Volga - not everyone comes back. Horde officials, the baskaks and census-takers, count the people and collect the "exit", the tribute. The shrewdest of all was Prince Ivan Kalita of Moscow (1325–1340): he gathers the tribute for the khan himself and buys up lands.
primer.rus_p_world_donskoy.title: Moscow rises
primer.rus_p_world_donskoy.text: Moscow is growing. Dmitry Ivanovich built a white-stone Kremlin (1367), and in 1380 on the field of Kulikovo he defeated the Horde ruler Mamai - for this he will be called Donskoy, "of the Don". But two years later Khan Tokhtamysh burned Moscow, and tribute had to be paid again. Under Vasily II (1425–1462) his uncle Yury and cousins Vasily Kosoy and Dmitry Shemyaka fight him for the throne for a quarter of a century; Vasily was blinded and became known as the Dark.
primer.rus_p_world_ivan3.title: The end of the yoke
primer.rus_p_world_ivan3.text: Grand Prince Ivan III is gathering Rus under Moscow's hand. In 1478 he subdued Novgorod and carried its veche bell off to Moscow, and in 1480 the Horde khan Akhmat stood on the Ugra river and withdrew without a battle - that was the end of the yoke. Ivan married the Byzantine princess Sophia Palaiologina, adopted the double-headed eagle, and Italian masters are building him a new Kremlin of red brick. His son Vasily III annexed Pskov, Smolensk and Ryazan.
primer.rus_p_world_ivan4.title: The reign of the Terrible
primer.rus_p_world_ivan4.text: Ivan IV, called the Terrible, is on the throne: in 1547 he became the first Moscow ruler to be crowned tsar. He took Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556), but the long Livonian War drained the country, and the oprichnina (1565–1572) brought executions and ruin; in 1571 the Crimean khan burned Moscow. After Ivan's death his son Fyodor reigns, and from 1598 Boris Godunov: the line of Rurik on the Moscow throne has died out.
primer.rus_p_world_novgorod.title: Lord Novgorod the Great
primer.rus_p_world_novgorod.text: Lord Novgorod the Great lives by its own rules. In 1136 the Novgorodians drove out Prince Vsevolod, and ever since they decide for themselves whom to invite as prince and whom to "show the road". What matters is the veche, an assembly summoned by a bell at Yaroslav's Court, which elects the posadnik (mayor), the tysyatsky (militia chief) and even the archbishop. The city grows rich on Hanseatic trade and northern furs, and in 1240–1242 Prince Alexander Nevsky beat back the Swedes and the German knights.
primer.rus_p_world_kiev_ruin.title: Kiev after Batu
primer.rus_p_world_kiev_ruin.text: In December 1240 Batu's army took Kiev after a siege. The papal envoy Plano Carpini, passing through in 1246, wrote that barely two hundred houses remained in the former capital and that skulls and bones lay in the fields around it. Governors now rule Kiev, and in 1299 even the metropolitan will leave for Vladimir in the north-east. Yet people come back, build new huts on the ashes and pray in the churches that survived.
primer.rus_p_society.title: Prince, boyars, smerds
primer.rus_p_society.text: At the top are the prince and his boyars, the senior druzhina, who are rewarded for service with villages and revenues. Below are the junior retainers, later the servitors, then merchants and the craftsmen of the posad, the trading quarter. Most people are smerds, peasants who plough the land and pay tribute. At the very bottom are the kholops, the unfree. Under the Russkaya Pravda every life has its price: killing a prince's man costs a fine of 80 grivnas, a free man 40, and a smerd just 5.
primer.rus_p_society_slave.title: Kholops
primer.rus_p_society_slave.text: You were born into a family of kholops - the unfree. People become kholops as captives, as debtors who sold themselves, or by marrying a kholop woman without an agreement with her master; kholops' children are kholops too. A master can sell you, and killing a kholop costs not a blood fine but only his price, as for a thing. Yet kholops differ: some plough a boyar's land, others run households as tiuns, stewards, and many are freed in their master's will "for the remembrance of his soul".
primer.rus_p_society_peasant.title: Smerds and Saint George's Day
primer.rus_p_society_peasant.text: Your family are smerds, peasants: a hamlet of a few homesteads in the middle of the forest. The forest is burned for fields - slash-and-burn: for a few years rye grows well in the ash, then the field is abandoned and a new patch burned. You pay the prince tribute in furs, honey and grain, later quitrent to a landlord. From 1497 a peasant may leave his lord only once a year, in the week before and after Saint George's Day in autumn, 26 November, after paying a fee for the years lived there - and from the 1580s even that right is often suspended.
primer.rus_p_society_noble.title: Boyars and servitors
primer.rus_p_society_noble.text: Your family belongs to the boyars and service people. A boyar is one of the senior druzhina, an adviser to the prince: he holds a votchina, hereditary land with villages, a tall wooden mansion with carved porches, and kholops of his own. In the Muscovite state servitors receive pomestie, land held for as long as they serve, and each must report for campaign "on horse, with men and with arms". Noble families jealously count their precedence: to sit at table below a man of lesser lineage shames the whole clan.
primer.rus_p_birth.title: Born in the bathhouse
primer.rus_p_birth.text: Babies are often born in the bathhouse - it is warm and clean there and, people believe, out of reach of the evil eye. A village midwife delivers the child, washes and swaddles it. Baptism usually comes within the first days or weeks, and the name is taken from the church calendar - a saint whose feast falls near the birthday. Besides a baptismal name many have a worldly, everyday one: Zhdan ("awaited"), Nezhdan ("unexpected"), Tretyak ("third"), Pervusha ("firstborn"). It is said to protect the child, since evil spirits will not learn its true name.
primer.rus_p_childhood.title: A cradle from the beam
primer.rus_p_childhood.text: A baby lies in a cradle hung from the matitsa, the main ceiling beam, and the mother rocks it with her foot while she spins. From spring to autumn children run barefoot, playing knucklebones and ball; in winter they sled down hills. From seven boys help their fathers in the fields, at fishing and in the forest, and girls spin and mind the little ones. In Novgorod children learn their letters: in the thirteenth century a boy named Onfim left his lessons on birch bark - the alphabet, syllables and drawings of warriors on horseback.
primer.rus_p_home.title: Hut and stove
primer.rus_p_home.text: Rus lives in wooden houses. An izba is a frame of pine logs, its gaps stuffed with moss, roofed with planks or thatch. In the middle stands a stove, long without a chimney: it is fired "black", the smoke spreading under the ceiling and escaping through a small sliding window, and the upper walls are black with soot. Windows are covered with ox bladder, or mica for the rich. Benches run along the walls, icons hang in the "beautiful corner", and every yard has its own bathhouse.
primer.rus_p_food.title: Cabbage soup and kasha
primer.rus_p_food.text: The table is built on rye bread, kasha and shchi, a soup of cabbage and turnips. People drink kvass, fermented honey mead and beer. Forests and rivers provide fish, mushrooms, berries and game; for winter cabbage is fermented, and fish and mushrooms are salted. There are about two hundred fast days a year, when people eat fish, mushrooms, peas and kasha cooked in hemp oil. No one has heard of potatoes, but everyone has turnips - hence the saying "simpler than a steamed turnip".
primer.rus_p_clothes.title: Shirt and bast shoes
primer.rus_p_clothes.text: Men wear a long shirt outside their trousers, belted with a sash; on their feet are bast-bark lapti over foot cloths, or leather boots for the rich. In winter they put on a sheepskin coat or a fur coat worn fur-side in, and a fur hat. Women wear a long shirt with a woollen skirt, the ponyova, later the sarafan; girls wear their braid uncovered, while married women hide their hair under a cap and kerchief - to be caught "bare-haired" is a disgrace. Boyars show off in coats lined with sable.
primer.rus_p_faith.title: A faith from Tsargrad
primer.rus_p_faith.text: Rus was baptised around 988, and its faith is Orthodox, from Tsargrad - Constantinople. Church domes gleam above the towns, and every hut has a corner with icons and a little lamp. Monasteries spring up across the land: the Caves Monastery in Kiev, the Trinity Monastery in the forests near Moscow, founded by Sergius of Radonezh. Services are in Church Slavonic, close to everyday speech. But old customs live on: pancakes at Maslenitsa, bonfires on Kupala night, and a domovoi, a house spirit, believed to live in every hut.
primer.rus_p_faith_pagan.title: The old gods
primer.rus_p_faith_pagan.text: Your family keeps to the old faith. The chief god is Perun the Thunderer; Vladimir once set up his idol in Kiev with a silver head and golden moustache. People also honour Veles, god of cattle, Mokosh, protector of spinning and women's fate, Dazhbog and Stribog. They pray in sacred groves and by holy stones, make offerings and hold funeral feasts for the dead. The volkhvs, priests and seers, are listened to, and in famine years, the chronicle says, they more than once stirred people against the new faith.
primer.rus_p_faith_jewish.title: The Jews of Kiev
primer.rus_p_faith_jewish.text: You come from the Jewish community of Kiev. Jews came here from Khazaria and with merchants from the East; they live by the Jewish Gate and trade with Constantinople, Germany and Poland. As early as the tenth century Kievan Jews wrote a letter in Hebrew that would later be found in the Cairo Geniza - one of the earliest mentions of Kiev at all. Life can be uneasy: in 1113, after Prince Sviatopolk died, rioting townsfolk looted Jewish homes.
primer.rus_p_faith_muslim.title: Tatars in service
primer.rus_p_faith_muslim.text: You are a Muslim - one of the Tatars serving the ruler of Moscow. Already under Vasily II Tatar princes began entering Moscow's service, and in 1452 the Kasimov Khanate on the Oka was founded for them. Tatar merchants and servitors live in Moscow with their own customs, and after the taking of Kazan (1552) there are many more Muslims in the realm. Some accept baptism and become Russian nobles: tradition says the Godunov family descends from a baptised Tatar named Chet.
primer.rus_p_faith_catholic.title: Latins in Novgorod
primer.rus_p_faith_catholic.text: You are a Latin, a Catholic - there are few of them in Novgorod. Most are German and Gotland merchants with their own courts: the Gotland Court with the church of Saint Olaf and the German Court, the Peterhof, with the church of Saint Peter. The Hansards bring cloth, silver, salt and wine and take away furs and wax. They live by their own statute, the Skra: at night the court is locked and watchdogs are let loose. Novgorodians call them nemtsy - "the mute ones", who cannot speak Russian.
primer.rus_p_work.title: Furs, wax and grivnas
primer.rus_p_work.text: The wealth of Rus is the forest: sable, marten and squirrel furs, wax, honey and flax. Fields are ploughed with a wooden sokha and sown with rye, oats and barley. In towns smiths, potters, tanners and jewellers work, and streets are named after crafts - Smiths' Street, Potters' Street. For a long time there is no native coin: people count in grivnas, silver ingots, and in kunas and rezanas, and in the twelfth to fourteenth centuries pay with ingots and furs. From the late fourteenth century Moscow mints dengi - from the Tatar word tenge.
primer.rus_p_place.title: Forests and rivers
primer.rus_p_place.text: Rus is endless forest, marsh and rivers that serve as roads: the route "from the Varangians to the Greeks" runs along the Volkhov and over portages to the Dnieper. Towns stand on high riverbanks behind earthen ramparts and wooden walls; inside is the detinets, or kremlin, with the prince's court and cathedral. Winters are long, with blizzards and hard frost, and in spring and autumn comes the rasputitsa, the mud season, when neither sledge nor cart can pass.
primer.rus_p_place_kiev.title: Mother of Rus cities
primer.rus_p_place_kiev.text: Kiev stands on high hills above the Dnieper. On the heights are the prince's court, the Church of the Tithes and Saint Sophia with its golden mosaic of the Virgin Orans, and the Golden Gate leads into the city. Below, in the Podil, the market bustles by the wharves, and in caves on the Dnieper bluffs live the monks of the Caves Monastery. The German chronicler Adam of Bremen called Kiev the rival of Constantinople and "the brightest ornament of Greece" - as the West called the Orthodox world.
primer.rus_p_place_novgorod.title: City on the Volkhov
primer.rus_p_place_novgorod.text: Novgorod straddles the Volkhov: on the Sophia Side stands the detinets with the Cathedral of Saint Sophia, on the Trade Side the market, Yaroslav's Court and the veche square, and between them the Great Bridge, where Novgorodians sometimes settle disputes with their fists. The streets are paved with logs, relaid every 20–30 years, so the centuries pile up underfoot. The damp earth preserves birch-bark letters - notes about debts, purchases, love and lessons.
primer.rus_p_place_vladimir.title: White-stone Vladimir
primer.rus_p_place_vladimir.text: Vladimir on the Klyazma is a city of white stone. Andrei Bogolyubsky made it the seat of the grand prince and built the Golden Gate and the Dormition Cathedral, and his brother Vsevolod the Big Nest built the Cathedral of Saint Demetrius, its walls covered with carved lions, griffins and saints. Nearby, on a water meadow, stands the Church of the Intercession on the Nerl. Around the city lies the Opolye, fertile open land where grain grows well. In February 1238 Batu's armies burned the city.
primer.rus_p_place_moscow.title: Wooden Moscow
primer.rus_p_place_moscow.text: Moscow stands on a hill where the Neglinnaya meets the Moskva river. Inside the Kremlin walls are cathedrals, the grand prince's palace and the court of the metropolitan, who moved here around 1325. Around it lie Kitai-gorod with its market, craftsmen's quarters, hundreds of wooden churches and yards with vegetable plots. The city burns to the ground again and again, and foreigners report that a new log house can be bought ready-made at the market, taken apart log by log. By the late sixteenth century Moscow is one of the largest cities in Europe.
primer.rus_p_law.title: The Russkaya Pravda
primer.rus_p_law.text: The law of Rus is the Russkaya Pravda, written down under Yaroslav the Wise and his sons. It replaced blood vengeance with the vira, a fine in grivnas, and truth is sought through witnesses, a sworn oath and the ordeal of hot iron or water. The prince or his tiun judges, while marriage and faith cases go to the bishop. Later, in Moscow, came the law codes of 1497 and 1550, and with them the knout, prison and the death penalty for robbery and treason.
primer.rus_p_health.title: Herbs, bathhouse, prayer
primer.rus_p_health.text: People heal with herbs, the bathhouse and prayer. Folk healers whisper charms, and monasteries have their healer monks; the most famous, Agapit of the Caves, is said in his Life to have cured Vladimir Monomakh himself. Fevers, smallpox and "pestilent winds" mow people down: in 1352 plague reached Pskov and Novgorod and spread further, and in Glukhov and Beloozero, the chronicle says, not a single soul was left alive. By estimates, one child in three does not live to five.
primer.rus_p_women.title: Wife and widow
primer.rus_p_women.text: Girls marry young, at about 13 to 16, by arrangement between parents; the dowry remains the wife's property. A wife runs the household, spins, weaves and raises the children, and a widow may manage property and even power herself: women have ruled since the days of Princess Olga, and in the fifteenth century Marfa the Posadnitsa led the Novgorod boyars against Moscow. In the Muscovite state noblewomen are kept ever more strictly in the terem, and the Domostroi, a household manual, teaches a husband to keep his wife obedient.
primer.rus_p_women_novgorod.title: Novgorod women on birch bark
primer.rus_p_women_novgorod.text: Novgorod women are surprisingly independent. Birch-bark letters show them reading and writing letters, lending money, trading and answering in court themselves. A woman named Anna asks her brother to defend her when she is slandered; Nastasya receives a note from her husband Boris asking her to send the shirt he forgot; and in the late thirteenth century Mikita writes to Ulyanitsa: "Marry me - I want you, and you want me." It may be the oldest marriage proposal in Rus.
primer.rus_p_leisure.title: Maslenitsa and minstrels
primer.rus_p_leisure.text: The great feasts belong to the Church, but many customs are older than Christianity. At Maslenitsa people bake pancakes, sled down hills and fight fist battles wall against wall; on Kupala night they leap over bonfires; at Yuletide they go about in masks. The skomorokhi - wandering musicians and jesters - dance, play the gusli and lead trained bears, though the Church scolds them. And everyone's favourite pleasure is the bathhouse with a birch switch, followed by a plunge into snow or the river.
primer.rus_p_knowledge.title: Books and birch bark
primer.rus_p_knowledge.text: Writing came to Rus with Christianity: the Slavic alphabet was created by Cyril, Methodius and their disciples, and books are written in Church Slavonic, which everyone can follow. Yaroslav the Wise gathered scribes and translators in Kiev, and around 1113 the monk Nestor compiled the Tale of Bygone Years. Books are costly - parchment is made from calfskin - but in Novgorod even ordinary people write on birch bark. In 1564 Ivan Fyodorov printed the Apostol in Moscow, the first precisely dated Russian printed book.
primer.rus_p_war.title: Steppe and abatis
primer.rus_p_war.text: The greatest threat is the steppe: Pechenegs, then Polovtsians, then Tatars raid villages and drive people off into captivity. Against them ramparts are raised and zaseki cut - barriers of felled trees across forest roads. A prince fights with his druzhina, horsemen in mail and helmets, and for a great campaign calls up a militia of voi. To the west are the Lithuanians, the Swedes and the German knights. Since 1550 Moscow has had streltsy armed with arquebuses and its own Cannon Yard.
